newsitem.title: ITALY: Italy's San Paolo clears decks for privatisation.
newsitem.headline: Italy's San Paolo clears decks for privatisation.

text.p: Italy's biggest commercial bank, Istituto Bancario San Paolo di Torino, currently owned by a public foundation, will be taken into private hands by mid-1997, San Paolo Chairman Gianni Zandano said Monday.

Zandano told a news conference in Turin that the bank planned to complete the privatisation, first started in 1992, by making a placement of around 20 percent of San Paolo's stock by the end of April.
The private placement with a core of Italian and overseas shareholders would be a prelude to a public offering of around 25 percent of the bank's capital to domestic and foreign investors.
"We hope if possible to complete (the privatisation) during the first half," he said.
None of the stable core of shareholders would own more than 5 percent of the bank, giving no single owner a pre-eminent position.

Zandano, who opposes the shareholder syndicates that have been a hallmark of Italy's closely knit business community, said he wanted a looser arrangement among core shareholders giving a bigger role to small investors and making the bank at least theoretically vulnerable to hostile takeover.
"We think the Italian market is mature and we are aiming to create a public company," Zandano said.

San Paolo's dominant shareholder, San Paolo Holding, with a 65.6 percent stake in the bank, will see its stake fall to no more than 20 to 25 percent after the privatisation, Zandano said. San Paolo Holding is wholly owned by Compagnia di San Paolo, a public foundation.

Other major shareholders in the bank include the Italian treasury, with 3.4 percent, Spain's Banco Santander with 3 percent and Italian investment bank Istituto Mobiliare Italiano (IMI) with 1.8 percent.
Zandano said he hoped both banks could be persuaded to exercise an option to raise their respective shareholdings to 5 percent each.
He was also hoping to woo Fiat, the automaker, and investors from France, Germany and possibly Britain into buying stock in the private placement.
